brief.title: Senate permitting bill S. 5653 and data center grid costs
brief.summary: S. 5653, the bipartisan permitting package introduced Sept. 30, 2026, would make large computing loads pay more of the cost of transmission. A Grid Strategies estimate puts that at about $55 billion over 10 years. A reported final manager's amendment keeps a 'large loads pay' rule for 20 MW+ loads ahead of a 60-vote cloture vote. That vote's outcome is unknown.
brief.origin:
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito introduced S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, on Sept. 30, 2026, with Sens. Lee, Whitehouse and Heinrich. It was referred to Senate Energy and Natural Resources.

The bill has two divisions:
- Division A: NEPA, Clean Water Act and ESA changes, plus 'project certainty' limits on revoking issued permits.
- Division B: transmission sections covering permitting (§2101), planning (§2103), an end to utilities' right of first refusal (§2105), 'ratepayer protection' (§2107), interconnection queue reform (§2110) and data collection on 'computational load entities' (§2114).

On Nov. 2, 2026, TechTarget reported a Grid Strategies estimate that the bill would shift about $55 billion in transmission costs to data centers over 10 years. Around Saturday, Nov. 7, senators reportedly released a final manager's amendment, with a cloture vote set for the following Monday (likely Nov. 9). That report is unconfirmed.
brief.causes:
Data-center demand growth is concentrated in PJM and MISO. It is raising grid investment needs and consumer power bills, which has made 'make data centers pay' a bipartisan affordability message.

The package appears to be a cross-committee deal. Republicans mostly want faster NEPA reviews and fewer lawsuits. Democrats mostly want more transmission and protection for ratepayers. This characterization is the researcher's inference.

States want to keep control over line siting and retail rates. That explains the reported one-year state-first window before FERC's backstop authority applies, and the §2107(b) 'Ratepayer Protection Floor' requiring states to address the generation costs large computing loads create.

brief.status:
The bill was introduced and referred to committee. A manager's amendment was reportedly released around Nov. 7, 2026. Reported provisions include:
- a one-year state-review requirement for 345 kV+ lines before FERC's backstop applies
- retention of the rule that new loads of 20 MW or more pay the full cost of serving them
- a new DOE Data Center Community Assistance Program

None of these details are verified. The result of the cloture vote (needs 60) is unknown. The $55B figure comes from an advocacy consultancy, not CBO or FERC. About 82% of the cost falls in PJM and MISO, and ERCOT is excluded. The estimate assumes new data centers buy firm transmission service.

brief.title: Senate permitting bill S. 5653 (BAAJA) and data center grid costs
brief.summary: S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, would speed federal permitting, expand FERC's role in interstate transmission, and make 20 MW+ computational loads pay the full incremental cost of serving them. It passed the Senate 62–33 on Nov. 19, 2026, and now goes to a House where passage is uncertain before Democrats take control in January 2027.
brief.origin:
Background, from the researcher's own knowledge and not checked: Manchin and Barrasso's Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 cleared the Senate energy committee in July 2024 but died. The House passed Rep. Westerman's NEPA-focused SPEED Act in December 2025. Both stalled.

Also in December 2025, Trump halted five offshore wind projects. Sens. Whitehouse and Heinrich then called permitting reform "dead in the water." Courts later ruled against the administration.

A deal came together in late September 2026. Utility Dive, citing Reuters, says it followed Trump assurances to Democrats on fair treatment for wind and solar. The bill lets developers sue over "disparate" federal treatment by project type.

Timeline:
- Sept. 30, 2026: Sens. Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich introduced S. 5653.
- Nov. 2: TechTarget reported a roughly $55B, 10-year transmission cost shift to data centers.
- Nov. 7: the sponsors released a substitute (manager's) amendment.
- Nov. 9: Senate voted 73–25 to begin debate.
- Nov. 16: Senate voted 70–27 to proceed on the substitute.
- Nov. 18: Senate voted 65–31 to end debate (cloture).
- Nov. 19: Senate passed the bill 62–33.
brief.causes:
AI-driven electricity demand is rising fast, and household power bills are going up. That has made "make data centers pay" a bipartisan affordability message, and the bill's sponsors frame it as holding big tech to its pledge not to shift costs onto other customers.

Energy projects of all types have long been slowed by permitting and litigation. Fossil and clean-energy developers both want faster, more predictable approvals.

The resulting trade:
- Republicans mainly get NEPA, Clean Water Act, ESA and NHPA streamlining and "project certainty."
- Democrats mainly get transmission reform, protection for wind and solar, and ratepayer safeguards.

States' interest in keeping control of siting and retail rates explains the state-first window before FERC's backstop siting authority applies.

actors.name: Sens. Capito, Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich (sponsors)
actors.role: Wrote the deal and steered it through the Senate. Capito and Lee pushed faster permits; Heinrich and Whitehouse pushed transmission, wind/solar protection and data-center cost accountability.
actors.stake: Getting a durable bipartisan permitting law enacted before the end of the year

actors.role: Thune brought the bill to the floor; Trump backs it and has promised to sign
actors.stake: Faster energy permitting and an affordability win

actors.name: FERC
actors.role: Would gain backstop authority to permit interstate lines after a year of state inaction, and would see its 1994 'higher-of' large-customer pricing policy overridden
actors.stake: Wider regulatory scope and implementation workload

actors.name: Data-center operators and hyperscalers
actors.role: As 20 MW+ computational loads, would pay full incremental generation, storage, transmission and distribution costs, plus financial guarantees, exit fees and liability for stranded costs
actors.stake: Effectively paying 'double' (embedded plus incremental costs), which changes the economics of siting, service type and on-site generation

actors.name: States and utility commissions
actors.role: Get first review of 345 kV+ lines before FERC's backstop applies, and handle large-load cost recovery at retail
actors.stake: Control over siting and retail rates

actors.role: 31 Democrats and 2 Republicans (Hawley, Rounds) voted no; green groups were split
actors.stake: Concern that the bill weakens environmental review and favors fossil fuels

brief.status:
Passed the Senate 62–33 on Nov. 19, 2026. It passed on the Nov. 7 substitute text only; changes negotiated in the final days were left out.

Data-center provisions:
- Loads of 20 MW or more pay the full incremental cost of serving them (reportedly §2107). That cost cannot be shifted to other customers.
- Large loads must post financial guarantees, pay exit fees, and remain liable for stranded costs if they leave.

Other reported provisions:
- FERC backstop permitting of interstate lines after a year of state review. Enverus says the introduced bill already allowed this after a year of state inaction, so how much the Nov. 7 text changed it (MLQ reports a 345 kV+ focus) is uncertain.
- A DOE Data Center Community Assistance Program and 20-year joint planning of transmission and generation. These come from search snippets only and are unverified.

The $55B (TechTarget) and $50B (explainx) cost-shift estimates have no verified author or assumptions.

Open questions:
- The House has not set a schedule or stated a position. Supporters had wanted 70–75 Senate votes to make House passage safe; the bill got 62.
- Per Axios, any final version must clear both chambers before the end of the year.
